name: Framing & anchoring

pinned_evidence.title: The Framing of Decisions and the Psychology of Choice
Judgment under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases
One Swallow Doesn't Make a Summer: New Evidence on Anchoring Effects
pinned_evidence.reason: replication/robustness — Maniadis, Tufano & List on anchoring reliability

evidence.basis: Framing: how equivalent information is presented shifts choice (Tversky & Kahneman 1981; Levin's attribute/risky/goal framing typology). Anchoring: an initial reference value biases subsequent estimates (Tversky & Kahneman 1974). Both robust, but anchoring's magnitude and some subliminal/incidental variants have a contested replication record.
evidence.effect_size_note: Framing effects are reliable, especially attribute framing. Anchoring is real and replicates for explicit/self-generated anchors, but incidental/subliminal anchoring is weaker and part of the replication debate; effect sizes vary widely by paradigm.

mechanism_summary_for_context: The same facts land differently depending on how they are framed and what reference point they are compared against. Two levers: framing (present the option in the terms that make its value salient — gain vs loss, what's included vs what's lost) and anchoring (set a reference value — a higher-tier price, a 'was' price, a recommended option — so other options are judged relative to it). Central to pricing pages, plan selection, and value presentation.

preconditions.reason: framing/anchoring operate on a presented choice, price, or value comparison; not applicable where there is nothing to frame

applicability.culture_note: Framing and anchoring are broadly universal; specific reference norms (what counts as a high anchor, culturally expected price presentation) are L3 surface parameters

implementations.generation_directive: Present a higher-value reference point before the target option so it is judged favorably: a premium tier shown first, a genuine 'was' price, or a recommended plan highlighted as the anchor. The anchor must be real (a genuinely offered tier or a true prior price) — fabricated anchors and fake 'was' prices are forbidden.

Frame the value in the terms that make it most salient and truthful — what the user gains, or (paired with LA-01) what they avoid losing. Attribute framing: present the positive attribute ('90% success' not '10% failure') where both are true. Never misrepresent — framing selects emphasis among true statements, it does not distort facts.

hard_rules.rule: Anchors (reference prices, tiers, 'was' prices) must be genuine; fabricated anchors and fake original prices are forbidden and often illegal
Framing selects emphasis among true statements; it must never misrepresent, omit material negatives deceptively, or state falsehoods
Decoy/reference options must be real offerings, not fake options designed solely to mislead

constraints.boundary_test: Is the frame emphasizing true value with a real reference point — or manufacturing a misleading comparison?

relations.note: Loss framing is the intersection of FR-11 (framing) and LA-01 (loss aversion) — presenting value as loss-avoided
Scarcity framing ('only 2 left') co-occurs with pricing presentation but is a distinct driver

orthogonality_note: Framing and anchoring are bundled as one L1 because both are presentation-of-choice effects operating at the same funnel point (pricing/selection); kept together for product coherence though they are distinct cognitive phenomena.

reference_examples.what: Middle 'most popular' tier anchored between a cheap and a premium option — canonical anchoring + decoy structure
Highest-capacity/priciest option shown first anchors perception so mid-tier feels reasonable
'Protect what you own' loss-framed vs 'save money' gain-framed — attribute/gain-loss framing at point of choice
